subject: chemistry
title: Rate & Equilibrium Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet reversible reactions and the magical idea of dynamic equilibrium.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry reversible reactions and equilibrium intro — Le Chatelier basics.
final_note: You now understand the ⇌ symbol and how an equilibrium responds to a nudge.

concepts.def: Products can re-form reactants — written with ⇌
Forward and backward rates are equal
Relative amounts of reactants vs products
System shifts to oppose any change applied

walkthroughs.body_html:
Some reactions go both ways.

The half-arrow symbol ⇌ means a reversible reaction. Reactants make products, and products can re-form reactants.

Example: ammonium chloride heats up to give ammonia + hydrogen chloride. Cool them and they recombine. NH₄Cl ⇌ NH₃ + HCl.

In a closed system, a reversible reaction reaches equilibrium. Both directions still happen, but at the same rate.

So the amounts of reactants and products don't change — even though particles keep reacting. That's why it's called dynamic.

It doesn't mean equal amounts of each. Just equal forward and backward speeds.

If you change the conditions, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.

Add more reactant? It shifts forward to use it up — more product made.

Remove product? It shifts forward to replace it.

The system always pushes back against whatever you do to it.

options: Forward and backward rates are equal

numericals.q: At equilibrium, the forward rate of reaction is 0.4 mol/s. What is the backward rate, in mol/s?
numericals.hint: At dynamic equilibrium the two rates are equal.

free_texts.q: If you add more reactant to an equilibrium, which direction does it shift to oppose the change? One word.
